name: Federal public lands

composition.note: One overlay drawn from three bundled files. Each member's features take the member's agency as their style key; a member with a `select` contributes only the features whose properties match it exactly. This file draws no features of its own while national wildlife refuges are withheld (see `refuges`). Every member file is split one part per feature, so an overlay added by viewport can skip whatever is off screen.

part_provenance: Each member file carries its own `source` member, copied into agencies.<agency>.source. No refuge tract ships (see `refuges`).
layer_caveats: Each colour on this layer is a jurisdiction: which federal agency's ground the publishing agency says a block is. It is not permission to hunt or to enter, and it is not a survey or a property line.

BLM land, BLM wilderness and national forest land are drawn together here, simplified for display to roughly 50 metres (BLM wilderness to roughly 10). Near an edge, treat this as a guide and not as your position relative to the real boundary. National wildlife refuges are not drawn on this layer.
Closures, fire restrictions, forest orders and refuge rules are invisible here. This layer shows ground, not today's conditions.
Unpainted ground is not shown, and it is not a claim of any kind. Land inside these boundaries that the agency does not hold, and every class of land this layer does not draw, is left blank.
Where two colours overlap, both are published: BLM wilderness sits on BLM land, and a block can be administered by one agency and held by another. Neither is merged into the other.

BLM.label: BLM-administered land
BLM.what_it_is: The Bureau of Land Management publishes this block as land whose surface it administers. It is BLM's own classification of the block, not a survey and not a finding of title by this app.
BLM.hunting_line: Hunting here is governed by California regulations as on other BLM land. Which agency administers the ground does not decide whether a hunt is legal — season, licence, tag, method and zone rules do, and they are quoted and cited elsewhere in this app.
caveats: BLM's own description of this data: “The SMA data do not illustrate land status ownership pattern boundaries or contain land ownership attribute details.” Where BLM administers a block another agency holds, the block names the holding agency.
Private inholdings that BLM's data carries are drawn as holes; one it does not carry is not shown at all.

BLM's own California cut is drawn as BLM publishes it and is not cut again by this app: 55 of its blocks lie outside CDFW's California county boundaries (offshore rocks, and parcels BLM's California office administers across the Nevada line).

source.doc: BLM National Surface Management Agency Area Polygons, BLM-only cut (gis.blm.gov lands/BLM_Natl_SMA_Cached_BLM_Only MapServer layer 2)
source.provenance: Copied from that file's own `source` member, built in the same run.

BLM wilderness.label: Designated Wilderness (BLM)
BLM wilderness.what_it_is: Congress has designated this area as wilderness and BLM administers it as part of the National Wilderness Preservation System.
BLM wilderness.hunting_line: Hunting here is governed by California regulations as on other BLM land. Wilderness rules restrict how you travel and what equipment you may use (43 CFR 6300), not whether you may hunt.
caveats: Designated wilderness only. BLM's wilderness study areas are not given this colour: they are not designated wilderness, and their ground is drawn as BLM land.
BLM publishes these boundaries as “generalized polygons”. They are drawn here at roughly 10 metres, from the same file as this app's separate BLM wilderness layer.
A wilderness can be administered by more than one agency, and this colour is BLM's portion only. Forest Service wilderness lies inside the Forest Service colour and is not coloured separately here.

source.doc: BLM National Landscape Conservation System Wilderness and Wilderness Study Areas, California cut (gis.blm.gov lands/BLM_Natl_NLCS_WLD_WSA MapServer layers 0 and 1)
source.provenance: Copied from that file's own `source` member, built in the same run.

USFS.label: National Forest System land (Forest Service)
USFS.what_it_is: The Forest Service classifies this block as land it owns and administers as part of the National Forest System. It is the agency's own classification of the block, not a survey and not a finding of title by this app.
USFS.hunting_line: Hunting here is governed by California regulations as on other federal land. Which agency administers the ground does not decide whether a hunt is legal — season, licence, tag, method and zone rules do, and they are quoted and cited elsewhere in this app.
caveats: This is a jurisdiction boundary, not a survey and not a property line. The Forest Service publishes it with the disclaimer quoted on this card, which says in the publisher's own words that it may not be used to determine ownership or boundaries.

This map draws Forest Service OWNERSHIP, not the proclaimed or administrative forest boundary. The two are very different: on Cleveland National Forest, 24.0% of the area inside the proclaimed line is not Forest Service land.

Land inside a national forest that is not Forest Service land is not drawn at all — neither the holes cut in these blocks nor, more often, the gaps between them. On Cleveland the holes account for about 38,900 acres while non-Forest-Service land inside the forest totals about 135,300, so most of it is in the gaps. Unpainted ground here is not shown, and it is not a claim of any kind.

Forest orders, temporary closures and fire restrictions are invisible here and this app does not carry them. They exist, they are current, and they can close roads, trails and whole districts. 36 CFR 261.50(f) states who to ask: "Any person wishing to use a National Forest System road or trail or a portion of the National Forest System, should contact the Forest Supervisor, Director, Administrator, or District Ranger to ascertain the special restrictions which may be applicable thereto."

This app cuts the Forest Service's national layer down to California against CDFW's county boundaries, and about 100 of the blocks drawn here were cut by that. On a cut block part of the edge you see is that cut and not the forest's own boundary — the state line on the Nevada and Oregon sides, the coastline on the Pacific side. The forest continues past it.

statutory_basis.label: The statute behind the words on this card
statutory_basis.framing: This app draws this boundary as a question of jurisdiction, not of permission, and the statute below is why the same words fit Forest Service land and BLM land. Read both subsections together: the first is quoted constantly on its own and means far less on its own than it appears to.

quotes.heading: In general
quotes.text: Subject to subsection (b), Federal land shall be open to hunting, fishing, and recreational shooting, in accordance with applicable law, unless the Secretary concerned closes an area in accordance with section 7913 of this title.

quotes.heading: Effect of part
quotes.text: Nothing in this subchapter opens to hunting, fishing, or recreational shooting any land that is not open to those activities as of March 12, 2019.

quotes.heading: Definition of “Federal land”
quotes.text: The term “Federal land” means— (A) any land in the National Forest System (as defined in section 1609(a) of this title) that is administered by the Secretary of Agriculture, acting through the Chief of the Forest Service; and (B) public lands (as defined in section 1702 of title 43), the surface of which is administered by the Secretary, acting through the Director of the Bureau of Land Management.

statutory_basis.closing: So a hunt is legal here for the same reasons it is legal anywhere else in California — season, licence, tag, method and zone — and the closures the first subsection points at are exactly the ones this map cannot show you.
statutory_basis.source_doc: Office of the Law Revision Counsel, United States Code (prelim), Title 16 §§ 7911–7912 (Pub. L. 116–9, title IV, §§ 4101–4102, Mar. 12, 2019, 133 Stat. 757)
statutory_basis.source_currency: Text contains those laws in effect on September 4, 2026

card.label: National wildlife refuge land (Fish and Wildlife Service)
card.what_it_is: The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's realty records classify this tract as national wildlife refuge land the Service holds in fee. It is the Service's own classification, not a survey and not a finding of title by this app.
card.hunting_line: This app carries no refuge rule of any kind. The statute this layer quotes for BLM and Forest Service land defines “Federal land” as those two classes only, so it is not a rule about this ground. The Service's own words on this card are the guidance this app can give: contact the refuge before you go.
caveats: The Fish and Wildlife Service's own words about this data: “Although these boundaries represent lands administered by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, not all areas are open to the public. Some fragile habitats need to be protected from human traffic and some management areas are closed. The public is urged to contact specific Refuges or other conservation areas before visiting.”

This layer draws refuge land the Service holds in FEE, and nothing else. Refuge land it holds by easement, lease, agreement or secondary jurisdiction is not drawn, so a refuge can be drawn in part or not at all. Easement land in particular is private land the Service holds a right over, and it is never painted here.
The Service's wildlife management areas, coordination areas and fish hatcheries are not national wildlife refuges and are not drawn.

This app cuts the Service's national layer down to California against CDFW's county boundaries, and 51 of the tracts drawn here were cut by that: on the Arizona and Oregon state lines, and along the shore of the ocean and San Francisco Bay, where those boundaries stop. The refuge continues past the cut. Because the boundaries stop at the shore, two California refuges are not drawn at all: Farallon Islands and Castle Rock.
